titles.l2: Finding one that breaks the rule

kernelIdea: ¬(∀x p(x)) is the same as ∃x ¬p(x), and ¬(∃x p(x)) is the same as ∀x ¬p(x). A single counterexample destroys a universal claim.

kernels.l1: To knock down an every claim, find one bad apple. Just one is enough.
kernels.l2: The opposite of an every telling is a some telling: one bad apple breaks it. The opposite of a some telling is an every telling: you have to check them all.
kernels.l3: The opposite of "every case works" is "some case fails," and the opposite of "some case works" is "every case fails." So one bad apple — a single counterexample — is enough to destroy a for all claim.
kernels.l4: ¬(∀x, p(x)) ≡ ∃x, ¬p(x) and ¬(∃x, p(x)) ≡ ∀x, ¬p(x). Negation swaps the quantifier and negates the predicate, so a single counterexample refutes a universal statement.
kernels.l5: Negating a quantified statement swaps ∀ with ∃ and negates what follows; applied to nested quantifiers, the swap happens at every level.
kernels.l6: Pushing ¬ inward through a quantified statement flips each quantifier in turn and negates what is left at the end. The ∃ that the negation produces is exactly the one bad apple you go looking for.
kernels.l7: Negation exchanges ∀ and ∃ and passes to the negated predicate — the De Morgan laws at infinite arity. Consequently refuting a universal statement means exhibiting a single counterexample.
kernels.l8: The quantifier duality ¬∀ ≡ ∃¬ is De Morgan duality for the infinitary meet and join; pushing negations inward to prenex normal form is the routine that makes quantified statements computable with.
